extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students and researchers in social theory, sociology/psychology of humour and cultural studies
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing and theorizing humour as a social phenomenon—its disciplinary functions, paradoxes, historical grounding, and ideological effects. The page develops criteria for evaluating accounts of humour rather than practical joke-writing advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary function of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter operates as a form of social discipline: it indicates inappropriate behaviour, teaches how to behave in public, and provides a model of ridicule that socializes novices (e.g., children) into norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Little Hans in the restaurant—adults laugh to signal and teach that staring is inappropriate. Implication: analyses of humour should assess how laughter enforces social codes and conveys normative instruction rather than treating laughter as merely innocent amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as concealment and self-reassurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that one is ‘just laughing’ or ‘just joking’ can hide cruelty and the disciplinary intent of ridicule; believing one is 'just laughing' helps the laugher avoid acknowledging the harm they cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humour, note whether performers or audiences frame laughter as innocuous while it functions to reassure and conceal aggression or disciplinary effects. Anti-pattern: accepting 'we were only joking' as evidence of harmlessness without examining consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adults' vicarious licence to transgress
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary laughter permits onlookers to enjoy the licence to perform the very behaviours they sanction (e.g., staring), producing a paradox where laugher both constrains and enjoys transgression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should consider how humour allows observers to vicariously perform forbidden actions and how that enjoyment coexists with enforcement of norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Laughing about it later' phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassing events that were painful at the time can be retold later as humorous stories; the retelling transforms past pain into present pleasure and recruits audiences to validate that transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features to identify: the original event was not funny at the time; retelling signals require hearer laughter; teller and hearers become observers of the past. Example transcripts (Kotthoff) show interpolated laughs; researchers should examine timing and ownership of laughter in retellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter-as-narrative-mode vs laughter-as-content
rubrics_metrics.description: In many 'laugh-about-it-later' stories the laughter is the mode of telling rather than part of the story content—the teller signals that hearers should laugh even if the original witnesses did not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humorous narratives, distinguish between content that describes laughter at the time and rhetorical moves that demand laughter in the retelling (e.g., 'you had to be there' effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox of discipline and rebellion
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour simultaneously enforces social order (discipline) and expresses pleasure at subversion (rebellion); the mechanism that ensures compliance may also produce delight in seeing it disrupted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical accounts should assess both functions: how a joke reproduces norms and how it provides vicarious rebellion. Example: practical jokes disrupt then reinforce order; comedians voice the unsayable yet may sustain existing hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embarrassment as social glue and generator of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear of embarrassment enforces compliance with social norms; ridicule is a mechanism through which embarrassment is learned and retained, making embarrassment central to the social ordering function of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include developmental perspective: babies are not embarrassed; children learn embarrassment partly through others' ridicule. Evaluate humour theories for their account of embarrassment's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freudian/repression perspective on humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Freudian idea that repression returns in jokes: humour often involves disruption of social codes and expresses repressed desires; joking can be a form of return of repressed impulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using psychoanalytic accounts, check for how repression, return of the repressed, and aggression are mobilized to explain humour. Also note Freud's omission of the disciplinary teaching of repression (adults provide models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of ideological positivism about humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Skepticism toward views that uncritically celebrate humour's positive benefits (health, social smoothing). The critical approach warns that humour's disciplinary/negative roles are often overlooked by optimistic accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should not assume humour is inherently therapeutic or progressive; instead evaluate claims of positive effects against evidence of humour's role in social control and power reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal vs particular grounding of humour theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories that present universal laws of humour (e.g., incongruity, superiority) must be situated in their historical/intellectual contexts; universal claims often mask their social origins and ideological commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars should historicize theories (e.g., Hobbes, Bergson) and avoid treating general theories as context-free laws. Expect to connect theoretical claims to the cultural/political milieu that produced them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to difference (culture/gender/ethnicity) rather than pure universalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal theories risk ignoring variation across cultures, genders, ethnicities; although humour may be universal in being possible in all cultures, its specific forms and targets vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical and theoretical accounts should examine particularities and not subsume diversity under broad universals. Anti-pattern: claiming a single invariant psychological mechanism without cross-cultural evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power dynamics and social divisions in humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is implicated in relations of power; ridicule can maintain social divisions (e.g., famous vs ordinary). Rebellious jokes may paradoxically validate the targets they mock (celebrity parody creates celebrity status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate who laughs at whom, the social status of targets/audiences, and whether jokes sustain or challenge hierarchies. Example: celebrity parody in mass media can confirm celebrity culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media, capitalism and the perpetual carnival
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary media create a continual 'carnival' of irreverence that fits capitalist needs for constant novelty and consumer desire; humour in media serves economic as well as social functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of contemporary humour should link comedic forms to economic structures (e.g., market-driven novelty, advertising mockery) and consider ideological implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate purported rebelliousness of humour for conservative functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent transgressive humour often performs conservative functions by channeling dissent into safe, marketable forms and by reinforcing the very distinctions (status, celebrity) it appears to mock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing political or rebellious comedy, check whether the humour actually undermines authority or simply reaffirms existing social orders; beware of concluding transgression from surface irreverence.
